name: Focal Distention
preview_text: Not all epigastric fullness is the same: the bloating that worsens with stress, the heavy feeling after overeating, and the dull ache that improves with rest each point to a differ...
synonyms: ["Localized Swelling", "Concentrated Distention", "Upper Abdominal Focal Distention", "Abdominal Focal Distension", "Epigastric Focal Distention", "Focal Distention In The Epigastrium", "Hard Epigastric Focal Distention", "Hard Focal Distention In The Epigastrium", "Hardened Distention In The Epigastric Area", "Hardened Focal Swelling In The Epigastric Region", "Firm Distention In The Upper Abdomen", "Firm Swelling In The Upper Abdomen", "Rigid Abdominal Distention In The Epigastrium", "Rigid Focal Distension In The Epigastrium"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, epigastric fullness is commonly associated with functional dyspepsia, gastroparesis, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. It describes a persistent sensation of uncomfortable fullness, pressure, or bloating in the upper central abdomen, often occurring after eating. Diagnosis typically involves ruling out structural causes through endoscopy or imaging, and may include gastric emptying studies if delayed stomach emptying is suspected.
Because the symptom often lacks a clear structural explanation, many patients receive a diagnosis of functional dyspepsia - a disorder of gut-brain interaction where the digestive tract functions abnormally despite normal test results. The approach focuses on symptom management rather than a cure for the underlying dysregulation.
conventional_treatments: Standard care includes dietary modifications (smaller, lower-fat meals), acid-suppressing medications (proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers), prokinetic agents to improve stomach emptying, and sometimes low-dose antidepressants to modulate gut-brain signaling. Antacids provide temporary relief, but the condition often persists or recurs.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands epigastric fullness primarily through the Stomach and Spleen, the two organs at the center of digestion. The Stomach is responsible for receiving food and sending it downward; the Spleen transforms food into Qi and lifts the clear, nourishing essence upward. When this rhythmic descent and ascent is disrupted, Qi stagnates in the middle burner - the area just below the ribcage - creating the sensation of focal distention or fullness.
The disruption can come from excess or deficiency. Excess patterns arise when something blocks the Stomach's downward movement: emotional stress causing Liver Qi to attack the Stomach, undigested food fermenting from overeating, or thick dampness and phlegm accumulating from poor digestion. In these cases, the fullness is often pronounced, may improve after belching or vomiting, and the tongue coating is thick or greasy.
Deficiency patterns occur when the Spleen and Stomach lack the energy to move food and fluids properly. Qi deficiency leads to a weak, sluggish distention that feels better with pressure and warmth, while Yin deficiency - a shortage of the Stomach's moistening fluids - creates a burning, gnawing fullness with a dry mouth. Because the same Western diagnosis can stem from such different roots, TCM always tailors treatment to the specific pattern, not just the symptom.
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by exploring the quality of the distention, what triggers it, and what eases it. Questions about diet, emotions, and energy levels help separate patterns. The tongue and pulse provide objective clues that confirm the picture.
If the distention flares with stress and is accompanied by frequent belching and a feeling of a lump in the throat, Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach is likely. The tongue often shows a thin white coating, and the pulse feels wiry, like a guitar string.
When overeating or rich meals bring on a heavy, bloated sensation with sour regurgitation and foul belching, Food Stagnation in the Stomach is the probable cause. The tongue coating becomes thick and greasy, and the pulse turns slippery, like beads rolling under the fingers.
Chronic distention that feels better with pressure, warmth, or rest, and is paired with poor appetite and fatigue, points to Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale and may show tooth marks on the edges, while the pulse is weak and deep.
A sticky sensation in the mouth, nausea, and a sense of heaviness in the abdomen suggest Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner. The tongue appears swollen with a thick, white, greasy coating, and the pulse is often slippery or wiry-slippery.
If the distention comes with a dry, bitter taste, sticky stools, and a feeling of heat, Damp-Heat in the Stomach and Spleen is indicated. The tongue is red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery.
When a burning discomfort accompanies the distention, along with dry retching and constant thirst, Stomach Yin Deficiency is the underlying pattern. The tongue looks red and peeled, with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Distention that radiates to the rib cage or sides", "Worsens noticeably with emotional stress or frustration", "Frequent belching or sour regurgitation", "Irritability, moodiness, or frequent sighing", "Sensation of a lump stuck in the throat (plum pit qi)"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, frustration, or anger, Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Alcohol, coffee, or sweet cocktails, Irregular eating or skipping meals, Rushing or eating while upset
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or movement, Deep breathing or meditation, Warmth on the abdomen, Small, light meals, Expressing emotions or talking it out
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress, frustration, or unexpressed anger causes the Liver Qi to stagnate and rise. Instead of flowing smoothly, it attacks the Stomach, disrupting its normal downward movement. This upward counterflow traps Qi in the epigastrium, creating the sensation of focal distention, bloating, and pressure that often radiates to the rib cage.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, may have redder sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), like a taut guitar string, especially strong at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate and then surge upward, invading the Stomach and blocking its descent. This is the core mechanism of the pattern, so calming the mind and smoothing Liver Qi immediately relieves the pressure. Gentle movement and warm compresses help move Qi locally, while heavy or irregular eating adds physical stagnation on top of the emotional one, worsening the distention.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, regular meals and avoid eating when upset. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi flowing. Prioritize stress management through deep breathing or meditation. Limit alcohol, coffee, spicy, and greasy foods, which can further irritate the Stomach.

patterns.symptoms: ["Epigastric distension that worsens after eating", "Sour, rotten-smelling belching", "Relief of bloating after vomiting", "Thick greasy tongue coating", "Aversion to food and its smell"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, large meals, or eating in a rush, Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Pressure on the abdomen, Eating late at night
patterns.better_with: Vomiting, Fasting or skipping a meal, Light, easily digested foods, Gentle abdominal massage
patterns.why_this_happens: When you overeat or consume heavy, greasy foods, the Stomach becomes overwhelmed and cannot digest properly. The undigested food sits and ferments, creating turbid Qi that blocks the normal downward flow of the Stomach. This obstruction causes epigastric fullness, distension, and sour rotten belching, especially after meals.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy, curd-like coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (滑 Huá) and full (实 Shí), especially forceful at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and heavy foods overwhelm the Stomach's digestive capacity, causing food to stagnate and ferment, which generates turbid Qi and blocks the middle burner. Vomiting expels the stagnant food, temporarily relieving the obstruction. Light diet and fasting allow the Stomach to recover its descending function, while gentle massage helps move Qi downward.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, lighter meals and chew food thoroughly. Avoid overeating, greasy or fried foods, and raw cold items. A short fast or skipping a meal can give the Stomach time to clear. Gentle walking after meals helps Qi descend.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull epigastric bloating that feels better with warmth and pressure", "Bloating worsens after eating", "Poor appetite with loose, unformed stools", "Persistent fatigue and weak limbs", "Pale, puffy tongue with tooth marks"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, large meals, or eating in a rush, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Physical overexertion, Worry and mental overwork
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Gentle pressure or lying down, Small, light meals, Rest and adequate sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Spleen and Stomach are the engines that turn food into Qi and move it through your digestive tract. When that engine weakens, it cannot transform and transport properly. Food and fluids sit in the middle burner instead of being processed, creating a sluggish, dull bloating that feels like a heavy ball just sitting there. Because the root is a lack of power rather than a traffic jam from rich food or anger, the distention is mild and chronic, and it often feels better with warmth or gentle pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and forceless, especially at the right Guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This is a true deficiency pattern-the Spleen and Stomach lack the Qi to process food and keep things moving. Warmth and rest conserve and support that fragile Qi, while cold, overeating, and exhaustion drain it further. Gentle pressure and lying down reduce the work the middle burner has to do, allowing the distention to ease naturally.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, soupy meals like congee with a little ginger; avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that demand too much digestive fire. Small, frequent meals are kinder than three large ones. Gentle daily walking supports Qi movement without draining you. Rest after meals and protect your belly with a warm compress when it feels heavy.

patterns.symptoms: ["Sticky, greasy feeling in the mouth", "No thirst or no desire to drink", "Heavy sensation in the body and limbs", "Nausea or feeling of queasiness", "Loose, sticky stools", "Bland or absent taste in the mouth"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or raw foods and drinks, Dairy, sweet, or greasy foods, Damp or humid weather, Overeating, large meals, or eating in a rush, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked foods, Gentle exercise or movement, Dry, warm environment, Small, light meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it cannot properly transform and transport fluids. These fluids accumulate into dampness and then condense into phlegm, which sits in the middle burner like a heavy fog. This phlegm-dampness blocks the normal descending of Stomach Qi and the ascending of Spleen Qi, creating a persistent feeling of fullness, stuffiness, and bloating in the upper abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, and a thick white greasy coating that is excessively moist. Pulse: slippery (Hua), often slow or moderate, and may feel soggy (Ru), especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-dampness is a heavy, turbid substance that forms when the Spleen is too weak to process fluids. Cold and raw foods directly damage Spleen Yang, while dairy, sugar, and greasy foods create even more dampness, worsening the blockage. Warm, cooked foods and spices gently support the Spleen's transforming function, helping to burn off the dampness. Exercise moves Qi, which in turn moves the stagnant fluids, much like a breeze clearing a fog.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet foods, as well as dairy, which all promote dampness and phlegm. Favor warm, cooked, easily digestible meals like soups, congees, and lightly steamed vegetables. Incorporate small amounts of warming spices such as ginger, cardamom, or black pepper to aid digestion. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps move Qi and dry dampness, while avoiding a sedentary, damp environment.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bitter or sticky taste in the mouth", "Heavy, sluggish feeling in the body and head", "Thirst with little desire to actually drink", "Sticky, incomplete bowel movements", "Dark, scanty urine"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Alcohol, coffee, or sweet cocktails, Hot, humid weather, Overeating, large meals, or eating in a rush, Dairy, sweet, or greasy foods, Prolonged sitting in damp places
patterns.better_with: Light, bland meals (congee, steamed greens), Bitter foods (bitter melon, dandelion greens), Dry, fresh air, Gentle exercise or movement, Barley or corn silk tea
patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and heat team up and settle in your stomach and spleen, like thick, sticky humidity on a hot day. This clogs the normal downward movement of stomach Qi and the upward movement of spleen Qi, trapping everything in the middle. The result is a heavy, bloated feeling in the upper belly, a bitter taste, and a body that feels sluggish and foggy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen with teeth marks, thick yellow greasy coating especially at centre and root. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu), often slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat is a combination of sticky moisture and simmering heat. Greasy, sweet, and spicy foods, along with alcohol, directly fuel that fire and gunk up your digestive system, while humid weather adds external dampness. On the other hand, bitter and bland foods naturally clear heat and drain dampness, much like a dry breeze clears a steamy room. Gentle movement keeps Qi flowing so it can transform and transport fluids, preventing them from stagnating into dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Steer clear of greasy, fried, spicy, and overly sweet foods, as well as alcohol and dairy-they all brew more damp-heat. Fill your plate with lightly cooked bitter greens, cucumber, celery, and barley. Sip warm water or mild barley tea, but avoid iced drinks which shock the spleen. A daily walk in fresh, dry air helps your Qi move and dries out internal dampness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Burning or gnawing sensation in the epigastrium", "Dry mouth and throat", "Thirst with a desire for small sips", "Dry retching or hiccups", "Feeling hungry but not wanting to eat", "Red tongue with little or no coating, dry centre"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried food, Alcohol, coffee, or sweet cocktails, Late nights and overwork, Emotional stress, frustration, or anger
patterns.better_with: Small sips of warm water, Moistening foods (pears, congee), Rest and adequate sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach depends on Yin fluids to stay moist and to guide food downward. When those fluids run low, the Stomach becomes dry and irritable, losing its healthy downward movement. Qi then stagnates in the upper abdomen, creating a feeling of stuffiness and focal distention. Because Yin deficiency often generates empty heat, the distention may carry a nagging burning quality, and the lack of moisture leads to dry mouth, dry retching, and a thirst that is only temporarily eased by small sips.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body, dry centre, little or no coating with possible cracks. Pulse: fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Yin Deficiency is a condition of dryness and heat from insufficient fluids. Spicy, fried, and alcoholic items are heating and drying, directly worsening the fluid deficit. Late nights and overwork drain Yin further, while emotional stress can stir up empty heat. In contrast, moistening foods and fluids gently replenish the Stomach's Yin, and rest allows the body to preserve and rebuild its depleted fluids, easing the burning distention.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent, moistening meals such as congee, millet porridge, steamed pears, and soft tofu. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Sip warm water or herbal teas like chrysanthemum throughout the day. Prioritise rest and avoid staying up late, which further depletes Yin.

faqs.question: What does acupuncture for epigastric fullness feel like?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture points for digestive issues are often on the abdomen, lower legs, and wrists. The insertion is typically shallow and gentle, with a mild ache or distending sensation around the needle that signals the Qi is responding. Most patients find the treatment deeply relaxing, and many report a softening of the abdominal tension even during the session.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I've been diagnosed with functional dyspepsia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Functional dyspepsia - where tests are normal but symptoms persist - is an area where TCM excels because it treats the functional imbalance directly. By identifying whether the root is Liver Qi stagnation, Spleen deficiency, or dampness, TCM addresses the underlying dysfunction rather than just suppressing acid or forcing stomach emptying. Many patients achieve lasting relief even when conventional approaches have offered little.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary adjustments are a key part of TCM treatment for epigastric fullness, but they are tailored to your pattern - not a one-size-fits-all list. In general, you'll be advised to eat warm, cooked foods, avoid overeating, and steer clear of greasy, raw, or cold items that tax the Spleen. Specific recommendations will follow your diagnosis, such as eliminating damp-forming foods or adding moistening foods for Yin deficiency.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: Many people feel a noticeable reduction in bloating and discomfort within the first 2-4 weeks of herbal treatment, especially for excess patterns triggered by stress or overeating. Chronic, deficiency-based fullness takes longer - often 2-3 months of consistent herbs and acupuncture - because the goal is to rebuild digestive strength, not just relieve symptoms. Your practitioner will track your tongue and pulse changes to gauge progress.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs with my antacids or prokinetics?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, but it's essential to inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about all medications and supplements you're taking. TCM herbs are generally compatible with acid reducers and prokinetics, but certain herbs may influence gastric emptying or acid secretion. A qualified practitioner will adjust the formula to avoid overlap or interaction, and may recommend taking herbs at a different time of day from your medications.

faqs.question: Is epigastric fullness during pregnancy treated differently?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many of the stronger Qi-moving or damp-draining herbs are avoided during pregnancy. TCM treatment during pregnancy focuses on gentle, safe methods - often dietary therapy, mild acupuncture (avoiding certain points), and very mild herbal formulas under close supervision. Always inform your practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive.

research.title: Acupuncture for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials found that acupuncture significantly improved dyspepsia symptoms and quality of life compared to sham acupuncture or conventional medication, with benefits lasting up to 3 months post-treatment. The effect was consistent across different acupuncture styles, supporting its use for epigastric fullness and discomfort.
research.periodical: Lan L, Zeng F, Liu GJ, et al. Acupuncture for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. 2015;2015:387196.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicine for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A comprehensive review of 49 RCTs involving over 6,000 patients found that Chinese herbal formulas - including those addressing qi stagnation, food retention, and spleen deficiency - were significantly more effective than placebo or prokinetic agents in reducing postprandial fullness, early satiety, and epigastric distention. Adverse events were mild and comparable to controls.
research.periodical: Liu J, Li X, Liu J, et al. Efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicine for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Pharmacol. 2020;11:601.
